title: Phase 4: SQL schema, EF Core and transaction boundaries
description: Design the SQL Server schema with proper indexes, foreign keys, soft-delete, and audit columns. Configure EF Core with owned types, value converters, and explicit transaction boundaries using the unit-of-work pattern.

data.text: The database schema is the longest-lived artifact in your system. A schema designed around CRUD convenience will become a liability when you need to add audit trails, multi-tenancy, or historical reporting. This phase locks in the physical model and the transaction guarantees your business logic depends on.

data.title: Principles
items: Every table has CreatedAt, CreatedBy, UpdatedAt, UpdatedBy, IsDeleted, DeletedAt for audit and soft-delete.
All foreign keys are explicit; never rely on conventions alone.
Natural keys (e.g., ExpenseReport.Id) are GUIDs; surrogate keys are identity ints for junction tables.
Covering indexes on high-frequency query paths; filtered indexes on IsDeleted = 0.

data.title: SQL: ExpenseReports table schema
data.content: Use SEQUENTIAL GUIDs (NEWSEQUENTIALID) for better index fragmentation than random GUIDs.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE Organizations (
    Id UNIQUEIDENTIFIER NOT NULL DEFAULT NEWSEQUENTIALID() PRIMARY KEY,
    Name NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    Slug NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    Currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    CreatedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME(),
    CreatedBy NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    UpdatedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NULL,
    UpdatedBy NVARCHAR(200) NULL,
    IsDeleted BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    DeletedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NULL
);

CREATE TABLE ExpenseReports (
    Id UNIQUEIDENTIFIER NOT NULL DEFAULT NEWSEQUENTIALID() PRIMARY KEY,
    OrganizationId UNIQUEIDENTIFIER NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Organizations(Id),
    EmployeeId UNIQUEIDENTIFIER NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES Users(Id),
    Status INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    TotalAmount DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    Currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    SubmittedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NULL,
    ApprovedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NULL,
    CreatedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME(),
    CreatedBy NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    UpdatedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NULL,
    UpdatedBy NVARCHAR(200) NULL,
    IsDeleted BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    DeletedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NULL
);

CREATE INDEX IX_ExpenseReports_Org_Status
    ON ExpenseReports (OrganizationId, Status)
    WHERE IsDeleted = 0;

CREATE TABLE LineItems (
    Id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    ExpenseReportId UNIQUEIDENTIFIER NOT NULL FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES ExpenseReports(Id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    Category INT NOT NULL,
    Amount DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    Currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    TransactionDate DATE NOT NULL,
    Description NVARCHAR(500) NULL,
    RequiresReceipt BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    CreatedAt DATETIMEOFFSET NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME()
);

CREATE INDEX IX_LineItems_ReportId ON LineItems (ExpenseReportId);

data.text: Configure owned types for Money, value converters for enums, and global query filters for soft-delete. Keep the DbContext in Infrastructure, not Domain.

data.title: C#: ExpenseDbContext configuration
data.content: Use Fluent API exclusively for complex mappings. Data annotations are fine for simple cases, but Fluent API keeps mapping logic in one place and survives model refactoring.

data.text: Unit of work and transaction boundaries

EF Core's DbContext is technically a unit of work and DbSet is a repository, but we wrap them in explicit abstractions for two reasons: testability (swap EF Core for an in-memory provider in tests) and explicit transaction control across multiple repositories.

data.title: C#: UnitOfWork implementation with ambient transaction
data.content: Begin a transaction at the handler level and commit only if all domain operations succeed.

data.title: Transaction scope matters
data.text: If a handler calls two repositories, and one fails after the other succeeded, you have a data integrity bug. Always wrap multi-repository work in an explicit transaction. MediatR pipeline behaviors are a clean place to do this automatically.

data.caption: Transaction boundary in ApproveExpenseReport flow
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as ApproveExpenseReportHandler
    participant R as IExpenseReportRepository
    participant E as ExpenseReport (Domain)
    participant U as IUnitOfWork
    participant D as Database

    H->>U: BeginTransactionAsync()
    U->>D: BEGIN TRANSACTION
    H->>R: GetByIdAsync(id)
    R->>D: SELECT ...
    D->>R: ExpenseReport
    R->>H: expenseReport
    H->>E: Approve(approverId)
    E->>E: Validate & raise domain event
    H->>R: UpdateAsync(expenseReport)
    R->>D: UPDATE ExpenseReports SET ...
    H->>U: SaveChangesAsync()
    U->>D: COMMIT TRANSACTION
    H->>H: Publish domain events

data.text: EF Core migrations are source-controlled and applied via `dotnet ef database update` in CI/CD. Seed data for roles, permissions, and default policy rules should be idempotent.

data.title: C#: Idempotent seed data
data.content: Seed methods must be safe to run multiple times without duplicating records.

items.text: SQL Server tables for Organizations, Users, Departments, ExpenseReports, LineItems, Approvals, PolicyRules, Receipts.
EF Core DbContext with owned types (Money), value converters (enums), and global query filters.
Soft-delete implemented with IsDeleted + DeletedAt + global filter.
Covering and filtered indexes for common query paths.
IUnitOfWork + ITransaction abstractions with EfCore implementations.
At least one integration test proving a transaction rolls back on handler failure.

data.title: Phase 4 summary
points: Schema is the longest-lived artifact — invest in indexes and audit columns now.
Soft-delete is non-negotiable for financial data; never hard-delete an expense report.
EF Core owned types map value objects cleanly to single columns or complex types.
Explicit transaction boundaries prevent partial writes when multiple repositories are involved.
data.takeaway: A well-designed schema makes the rest of the application easier. A poorly designed one forces you to add triggers, compensating transactions, or application-level rollbacks later.
